div.head: MEMB. 3. SUBSECT. 1.
Symptoms or signs of Love-Melancholy, in Body, Mind, good, bad, &c.
div.p: Symptoms are either of Body or Mind; of body, paleness, leanness, dryness, &c. Ovid. Facit hunc amor ipse colorem [It’s love itself that produces this colour], Met. 4.Pallidus omnis amans, color hic est aptus amanti [All in love are pale: it’s the right colour for the lover], as the Poet describes lovers: fecit amor maciem, love causeth leanness. Avicenna de Ilishi cap. 23 makes hollow eyes, dryness, Symptoms of this disease, to go smiling to themselves, or acting as if they saw or heard some delectable object. Valleriola lib. 2 observat. cap. 7, Laurentius cap. 10, Aelianus Montaltus de Her. amore, Langius epist. 24 lib. 1 epist. med. deliver as much, corpus exangue pallet, corpus gracile, oculi cavi [the bloodless body blanches, a thin body, hollow eyes], lean, pale,

lg.l: ——— ut nudis qui pressit calcibus anguem,
[… like someone with bare feet who’s stepped on a snake,]

div.p: hollow-eyed, their eyes are hidden in their heads,

l.hi: Tenerque nitidi corporis cecidit decor,

lg.l: [And the delicate beauty of the healthy body decayed,]

div.p: they pine away, and look ill with waking, cares, sighs,

l.hi: Et qui tenebant signa Phoebeae facis

lg.l: Oculi, nihil gentile nec patrium micant.
[And her eyes, which bore the traces of the torch of Phoebus,
Have none of the gleam of her family or her father.]

div.p: With groans, griefs, sadness, dullness,

lg.l: ——— Seneca Hippol.Nulla jam Cereris subit
Cura aut salutis ———
[… now she has no care
For food or health …]

div.p: want of appetite, &c. A reason of all this, De morbis cerebri de erot. amore.Jason Pratensis gives, because of the distraction of the spirits the Liver doth not perform his part, nor turns the aliment into blood as it ought, and for that cause the members are weak for want of sustenance, they are lean and pine, as the herbs of my garden do this month of May, for want of rain. The green sickness therefore often happeneth to young women, a Cachexia or an evil habit to men, besides their ordinary sighs, complaints and lamentations, which are too frequent. As drops from a still,

lg.l: ——— ut occluso stillat ab igne liquor,
[… just as water trickles from a banked fire,]

div.p: doth Cupid’s fire provoke tears from a true Lover’s eyes.

l.hi: The mighty Mars did oft for Venus shriek,
Privily moistening his horrid cheek,

lg.l: With womanish tears, ———
——— Amator. Emblem. 3.ignis distillat in undas,

l.hi: Testis erit largus qui rigat ora liquor,

lg.l: [… fire is distilled into water,
As the abundant liquid drenching his face will attest,]

div.p:
with many such-like passions. When Chariclea was enamoured on Theagenes, as Lib. 4.Heliodorus sets her out, she was half-distracted, and spake she knew not what, sighed to herself, lay much awake and was lean upon a sudden: and when she was besotted on her son-in-law, Apuleius.pallor deformis, marcentes oculi, &c., she had ugly paleness, hollow eyes, restless thoughts, short wind, &c. Aeneas. Silv.Euryalus in an Epistle sent to Lucretia his Mistress, complains amongst other grievances, tu
mihi & somni & cibi usum abstulisti, thou hast taken my stomach and my sleep from me. So Chaucer in the Knight’s tale.he describes it aright;

foreign.hi: His sleep, his meat, his drink, is him bereft,
That lean he waxeth, and dry as a shaft,
His eyes hollow and grisly to behold,
His hue pale and ashen to unfold,
And solitary he was ever alone,
And waking all the night making moan.

div.p: Theocritus Idyl. 2 makes a fair maid of Delphos in love with a young man of Myndus, confess as much,

l.hi: Ut vidi ut insanii, ut animus mihi male affectus est,
Miserae mihi forma tabescebat, neque amplius pompam
Ullam curabam, aut quando domum redieram
Novi, sed me ardens quidam morbus consumebat,
Decubui in lecto dies decem, & noctes decem,
Defluebant capite capilli, ipsaque sola reliqua

lg.l: Ossa & cutis. ———
No sooner seen I had, but mad I was,
My beauty fail’d, and I no more did care
For any pomp, I knew not where I was,
But sick I was, and evil I did fare,
I lay upon my bed ten days and nights,
A Skeleton I was in all men’s sights.

div.p: All these passions are well-expressed by Virg. 4 Aen.that Heroical Poet in the person of Dido;

l.hi: At non infaelix animi Phoenissa, nec unquam
Solvitur in somnos, oculisque ac pectore amores
Accipit; ingeminant curae, rursusque resurgens

lg.l: Saevit amor, &c. ———
Unhappy Dido could not sleep at all,
But lies awake, and takes no rest:
And up she gets again, whilst care and grief,
And raging love torments her breast.

div.p:
Accius Sannazarius Ecloga 2 de Galatea, in the same manner feigns his Lycoris Dum vaga passim sydera fulgent, numerat longas tetricus horas, & sollicito nixus cubito suspirando viscera rumpit [While the wandering stars are glittering far and wide, she gloomily counts the long hours, and the pain rends her insides as she lies down mournfully with a sigh].tormenting herself for want of sleep, sighing, sobbing, and lamenting; and Eustathius his Ismenias much troubled, and panting at heart, at the sight of his
mistress, he could not sleep, his bed was thorns. Gordonius cap. 20. Amittunt saepe cibum, potum, & maceratur inde totum corpus [They often send away food and drink, and then the whole body is wasted away].All make leanness, want of appetite, want of sleep ordinary Symptoms, and by that means they are brought often so low, so much altered and changed, that as Ter. Eunuch.he jested in the Comedy, one can scarce know them to be the same men.

l.hi: Attenuant juvenum vigilatae corpora noctes,

lg.l: Curaque & immenso qui fit amore dolor.
[Sleepless nights weaken youthful bodies,
And care, and the pain of a great love.]

div.p: Many such Symptoms there are of the Body to discern lovers by,

lg.l: ——— Ovid. Epist. 12.quis enim bene celet amorem?
[… for who can fully hide love?]

div.p: Can a man saith Solomon, Prov. 6. 27, carry fire in his bosom and not burn? It will hardly be hid, though they do all they can to hide it, it must out,

lg.l: plus quam mille notis ———
[by more than a thousand signs …]

div.p: it may be described,

l.hi: Quoque magis tegitur, tectus magis aestuat ignis,

lg.l: [The more the fire is covered, the more it burns,]

div.p:
’twas Antiphanes the Comedian’s observation of old, Love and drunkenness cannot be concealed, Celare alia possis, haec praeter duo, vini potum, &c. [you can hide everything apart from these two: wine-drinking, etc.], words, looks, gestures, all will betray them: but two of the most notable signs are observed by the pulse and Countenance. When Antiochus the son of Seleucus was sick for Stratonice his Mother-in-law, and would not confess his grief, or the cause of his disease, Erasistratus the Physician found him by his Pulse and Countenance, to be in love with her, Plutarch.because that when she came in presence, or was named, his pulse varied, and he blushed besides. In this very sort was the love of Charicles, the son of Polycles, discovered by Panacius the Physician, as you may read the story at large in Epist. 13.Aristaenetus. By the same sign Galen brags, that he found out Justa, Boethius the Consul’s wife, to dote on Pylades the Player, because at his name still she both altered Pulse and Countenance, as Barc. lib. 1.Poliarchus did at the name of Argenis. Franciscus Valesius, lib. 3 controv. 13 med. contr. denies there is any such pulsus amatorius [lover’s pulse], or that love may be so discerned; but Avicenna confirms this of Galen out of his
experience, lib. 3 Fen 1, and Gordonius, cap. 20, Their pulse he saith is inordinate and swift, if she go by whom he loves, Langius Epist. 24 lib. 1 med. Epist., Nevisanus lib. 4 numer. 66 syl. nuptialis, Valescus de Taranta, Guainerius, Tract. 15. Valleriola sets down this for a Symptom, Difference of Pulse, neglect of business, want of sleep, often sighs, blushings, when there is any speech of their Mistress, are manifest signs. But amongst the rest, Josephus Struthius that Polonian, in the fifth Book cap. 17 of his Doctrine of Pulses, holds that this and all other passions of the mind, may be discovered by the Pulse. And if you will know, saith he, whether the men suspected be such or such, touch their arteries, &c. And in his fourth Book, 14th Chapter, he speaks of this particular Pulse, Love makes an unequal pulse, &c., he gives instance of a Gentlewoman, a Patient of his, whom by this means he found to be much enamoured, and with whom: he named many persons, but at the last when his name came whom he suspected, her pulse began to vary, and to beat swifter, and so by often feeling her pulse, he perceived what the matter was. Apollonius Argonaut. lib. 4, poetically setting down the meeting of Jason and Medea, makes them both to blush at one another’s sight, and at the first they were not able to speak.

lg.l: ——— Eunuch. Act. 2 scen. 2.totus Parmeno

l.hi: Tremo, horreoque postquam aspexi hanc,

lg.l: [… I’m shaking all over, Parmeno,
Now that I’ve seen her I’m trembling,]

div.p: Phaedria trembled at the sight of Thais, others sweat, blow short,

lg.l: Crura tremunt ac poplites, ———
[The legs and knees quiver …]

div.p: are troubled with palpitation of heart upon the like occasion, cor proximum ori, saith Epist. 7 lib. 2. Tener sudor, & creber anhelitus, palpitatio cordis, &c. [A mild sweat and frequent panting, palpitation of the heart, etc.]Aristaenetus, their heart is at their mouth, leaps, these burn and freeze (for love is fire, ice, hot, cold, itch, fever, frenzy, pleurisy, what not), they look pale, red, and commonly blush at their first congress; and sometimes through violent agitation of spirits, bleed at nose, or when she is talked of: which very sign Lib. 1.Eustathius makes an argument of Ismene’s affection, that when she met her Sweetheart by chance, she changed her countenance, to a Maiden blush. ’Tis a common thing amongst Lovers, as Lexoviensis Episcopus [The bishop of Lisieux].Arnulphus that merry-conceited Bishop, hath well expressed in a facete Epigram of his,

l.hi: Alterno facies sibi dat responsa rubore,

lg.l: Et tener affectum prodit utrique pudor, &c.
Their faces answer, and by blushing say,
How both affected are, they do bewray.

div.p: But the best conjectures are taken from such symptoms as appear when they are both present; all their speeches, amorous glances, actions, lascivious gestures will bewray them, they cannot contain themselves, but that they will be still kissing. Theodorus Prodromus dial. Gaulmino Interpret.Stratocles the Physician upon his Wedding-day, when he was at dinner, nihil prius sorbillavit, quam tria basia puellae pangeret [wouldn’t sip anything before planting three kisses on the girl], could not eat his meat for kissing the Bride, &c. First a word, and then a kiss, then some other Compliment, and then a kiss, then an idle question, then a kiss, and when he hath pumped his wits dry, can say no more, kissing and colling are never out of season,

l.hi: Hoc non deficit incipitque semper,

lg.l: [It doesn’t run out, and it’s always starting,]

div.p: ’tis never at an end, Sed unum ego usque & unum Petam a tuis labellis, Postque unum & unum & unum, Unum dari rogabo [But I’ll demand one kiss, and again one from your lips, and after that I’ll ask to be given one more and one more and one more]. Leochaeus Anacreon.another kiss, and then another, another, and another, &c.

lg.l: ——— huc ades O Thelayra ———
[… Come here, Thelayra …]

l.hi: Centum basia centies,
Centum basia millies,
Mille basia millies,
Et tot millia millies,
Quot guttae Siculo mari,
Quot sunt sydera coelo,
Istis purpureis genis,
Istis turgidulis labris,
Ocellisque loquaculis,
Figam continuo impetu;

lg.l: O formosa Neaera.
[A hundred times a hundred kisses,
A hundred times a thousand kisses,
A thousand times a thousand kisses,
And as many thousand thousand times
As there are drops in the sea of Sicily,
As there are stars in the sky,
I’ll press passionately, incessantly, on to
Those rosy cheeks,
Those full lips,
And those speaking eyes;
O beautiful Neaera!]

div.p: As Catullus to Lesbia,

l.hi: Da mihi basia mille, deinde centum,
Dein mille altera, da secunda centum,
Dein usque altera millia, deinde centum,

lg.l: ——— Translated or imitated by Mr. B. Jonson, our arch-Poet in his 119th Ep.first give an hundred,
Then a thousand, then another
Hundred, then unto the other
Add a thousand, and so more, &c.

div.p: till you equal with the store, all the grass, &c. So Venus did by her Adonis, the Moon with Endymion, they are still dallying and Heinsius.culling, as so many Doves,

l.hi: Columbatimque labra conserentes labiis,

lg.l: [Joining lips to lips like doves pecking,]

div.p: and that with alacrity and courage,

l.hi: Affligunt avide corpus, junguntque salivas

lg.l: Oris, & inspirant prensantes dentibus ora.
[They greedily throw their bodies together, mingle the saliva from their mouths,
And draw deep breaths with teeth pressing on lips.]

div.p: Lucian. dial. Tom. 4 Meret.Tam impresso ore ut vix inde labra detrahant, cervice reclinata [With mouths pressed together so hard that they could hardly pull their lips apart, with necks bent back], as Lamprias in Lucian kissed Thais, Philippides her Epist. 16.in Aristaenetus, amore lymphato tam furiose adhaesit, ut vix labra solvere esset, totumque os mihi contrivit [crazy with love, he clung to me so madly that our lips could hardly be parted, and he exhausted my whole mouth]; Deducto ore longo me basio demulcet [With pursed lips, he turned me on with a long kiss].Aretine’s Lucretia, by a suitor of hers was so saluted, and ’tis their ordinary fashion.

lg.l: ——— dentes illudunt saepe labellis,
Atque premunt arcte adfigentes oscula ———
[… The teeth often play around with the lips,
And grip them tightly in planting a kiss …]

div.p:
They cannot, I say, contain themselves, they will be still not only joining hands, kissing, but embracing, treading on their toes, &c., diving into their bosoms, and that libenter, & cum delectatione [eagerly, and with delight], as In delitiis. Mammas tuas tango, &c. [I touch your breasts, etc.]
Philostratus confesseth to his Mistress; and Lamprias in Tom. 4 meret. dial.Lucian, mammillas premens, per sinum clam dextra, &c. [touching the nipple, with his right hand furtively touching the bosom, etc.], feeling their paps, and that scarce honestly sometimes: as the old man in the Terent.Comedy well observed of his son, Non ego te videbam manum huic puellae in sinum inserere? Did I not see thee put thy hand into her bosom? Go to, with many such love-tricks. Juno in Lucian, deorum Tom. 3 dial. 3, complains to Jupiter of Ixion, he looked so attentively on her, and sometimes would sigh and weep in her company, and when I drank by chance, and gave Ganymede the cup, he would desire to drink still in the very cup that I drank of, and in the same place where I drank, and would kiss the cup, and look steadily on me, and sometimes sigh, and then again smile. If it be so they cannot come near to dally, have not that opportunity, familiarity, or acquaintance to confer and talk together; yet if they be in presence, their eye will bewray them: ubi amor ibi oculus, as the common saying is, where I look I like, and where I like I love; but they will lose themselves in her looks.

l.hi: Alter in alterius jactantes lumina vultus,

lg.l: Quaerebant taciti noster ubi esset amor.
[Each, glancing at the other’s face,
Silently questioned, ‘Where might our love be?’]

div.p: They cannot look off whom they love, they will impregnare eam ipsis oculis, deflower her with their eyes, be still gazing, staring, stealing faces, smiling, glancing at her, as Quique omni cernere debes Leucothoen spectas, & virgine figis in una quos mundo debes oculos [You, who should observe everything, contemplate Leucothoe alone, and fix your eyes, which you ought to have on the whole world, on one virgin]. Ovid. Met. 4.Apollo on Leucothoe, the Moon on her Lucian. tom. 3. Quoties ad Cariam venis currum sistis, & desuper aspectas [Whenever you come to Caria you stop your chariot and look down from above].Endymion, when she stood still in Caria, and at Latmos caused her Chariot to be stayed. They must all stand and admire, or if she go by, look after her as long as they can see her, she is animae auriga [the soul’s charioteer], as Anacreon calls her, they cannot go by her door or window, but as an Adamant, she draws their eyes to it, though she be not there present, they must needs glance that way, and look back to it. Aristaenetus of Ex quo te primum vidi Pythia, alio oculos vertere non fuit [From the time that I first saw you, Pythias, my eyes would turn nowhere else].Euxitheus, Lucian in his Imagin. of himself, and Tatius of Clitophon say as much, Ille oculos de Leucippe Lib. 4.nunquam dejiciebat [he never took his eyes off Leucippe], and many Lovers confess when they came in their mistress’ presence, they could not hold off their eyes, but looked wistly and steadily on her, inconnivo aspectu [with unblinking gaze], with much eagerness and greediness, as if they would look through, or should never have enough sight of her.

lg.l: ——— Fixis ardens obtutibus haeret;
[… He’s brought to a stand-still, ardent with staring eyes;]

div.p: so she will do by him, drink to him with her eyes, nay drink him up, devour him, swallow him, as Martial’s Mamurra is remembered to have done:

lg.l: Inspexit molles pueros, oculisque comedit, &c.
[He examined the delicate boys, and devoured them with his eyes, etc.]

div.p: There is a pleasant story to this purpose in Navigat. Vertom. lib. 3 cap. 5. The Sultan of Sana’s wife in Arabia, because Vertomannus was fair and white could not look off him, from Sunrising to Sunsetting, she could not desist, she made him one day come into her chamber, & geminae horae spatio intuebatur, non a me unquam aciem oculorum avertebat, me observans veluti Cupidinem quendam [and for a couple of hours she stared, never turning her eyes from me, watching me as if I were some kind of Cupid], for two hours’ space she still gazed on him. A young man in Dial. Amorum.Lucian fell in love with Venus’ picture, he came every morning to her Temple, and there continued all day long from Sunrising to Sunset, unwilling to go home at night, sitting over against the Goddess’ Picture, he did continually look upon her, and mutter to himself I know not what. If so be they cannot see them whom they love, they will still be walking and waiting about their Mistress’ doors, taking all opportunity to see them, as in Lib. 3.Longus Sophista, Daphnis and Chloe two Lovers, were still hovering at one another’s gates, he sought all occasions to be in her company, to hunt in Summer, and catch Birds in the Frost about her Father’s house in the winter, that she might see him, and he her. A King’s Palace was not so diligently attended, saith Aretine’s Lucretia, as my house was when I lay in Rome, the Porch and street was ever full of some, walking or riding, on set purpose to see me, their eye was still upon my window, as they passed by, they could not choose but look back to my house when they were past, and sometimes hem or cough, or take some impertinent occasion to speak aloud, that I might look out and observe them. ’Tis so in other places, ’tis common to every Lover, ’tis all his felicity to be with her, to talk with her, he is never well but in her company, and will walk Lib. 3 Theat. mundi.seven or eight times a day through the street where she dwells, and make sleeveless errands to see her; plotting still where, when, and how to visit her,

l.hi: Lenesque sub nocte susurri,

lg.l: Composita repetuntur hora.
[And faint whispers in the night,
Resumed at the hour agreed.]

div.p: And when he is gone, he thinks every minute an hour, every hour as long as a day, ten days a whole year, till he see her again.

lg.l: Ovid.Tempora si numeres, bene quae numeramus amantes.
[If you count the hours, which we lovers count well.]

div.p: And if thou be in love, thou wilt say so too, Et longum formosa vale [and a long farewell, my beauty], farewell Sweetheart, vale charissima Argenis, &c., farewell my dear Argenis, once more farewell, farewell. And though he is to meet her by compact, and that very shortly, perchance tomorrow, yet loath to depart, he’ll take his leave again, and again, and then come back again, look after, and shake his hand, wave his hat afar off. Now gone, he thinks it long till he see her again, and she him, the clocks are surely set back, the hour’s past,

l.hi: Hospita Demophoon tua te Rhodopeia Phillis,

lg.l: Ultra promissum tempus abesse queror.
[Phyllis, your Thracian friend, complains to you, Demophoon,
That you’ve been away longer than you promised.]

div.p: She looks out at window still to see whether he come, Hyginus fab. 59.and by report Phyllis went nine times to the Seaside that day, to see if her Demophoon were approaching, and Chaucer.Troilus to the City gates, to look for his Criseyde. She is ill at ease, and sick till she see him again, peevish in the meantime, discontent, heavy, sad, and why comes he not? Where is he? Why breaks he promise? Why tarries he so long? Sure he is not well; sure he hath some mischance, sure he forgets himself and me, with infinite such. And then confident again, up she gets, out she looks, listens and enquires, harkens, kens, every man afar off is sure he, every stirring in the street, now he is there, that’s he, male aurorae, male soli dicit, dejeratque, &c. [she curses the dawn, curses the sun, and swears, etc.], the longest day that ever was, so she raves, restless and impatient; for Amor non patitur moras, Love brooks no delays: the time’s quickly gone that’s spent in her company, the miles short, the way pleasant, all weather is good whilst he goes to her house, heat or cold, though his teeth chatter in his head, he moves not, wet or dry, ’tis all one, wet to the skin, he feels it not, cares not at least for it, but will easily endure it and much more, because it is done with alacrity, and for his Mistress’ sweet sake; let the burden be never so heavy, Love makes it light. Gen. 29. 20.Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and it was quickly gone because he loved her. None so merry, if he may happily enjoy her company, he is in heaven for a time; and if he may not, dejected in an instant, solitary, silent, he departs weeping, lamenting, sighing, complaining.

But the Symptoms of the mind in Lovers, are almost infinite, and so diverse, that no Art can comprehend them; though they be merry sometimes, and rapt beyond themselves for joy: yet most part, Love is a plague, a torture, an hell, a bitter-sweet passion at last; Plautus Cistel.Amor melle & felle est faecundissimus, gustum dat
dulcem & amarum [love is most abundant with honey and gall, its taste is sweet and bitter]. ’Tis suavis amaricies, dolentia delectabilis, hilare tormentum [sweet bitterness, pleasurable pain, joyful torture];

l.hi: Et me melle beant suaviora,
Et me felle necant amariora;

lg.l: [And they bless me with more sweetness than honey,
And they destroy me with more bitterness than gall;]

div.p: like a summer fly or Sphinx’s wings, or a rainbow of all colours,

l.hi: Quae ad solis radios conversae aurae erant,
Adversus nubes caeruleae, quale jubar Iridis,

lg.l: [When turned to the sun’s rays the wings were golden,
Facing the clouds they were azure, as splendid as the rainbow,]

div.p: fair, foul, and full of variation, though most part irksome and bad. For in a word, the Spanish inquisition is not comparable to it; a torment and Plautus. Credo ego ad hominis carnificinam amorem inventum esse [I believe that among men the job of hangman was invented by love].execution it is, as he calls it in the poet, an unquenchable fire, and what not? De civitat. lib. 22 cap. 22.From it, saith Austin, arise biting cares, perturbations, passions, sorrows, fears, suspicions, discontents, contentions, discords, wars, treacheries, enmities, flattery, cozening, riot, lust, impudence, cruelty, knavery, &c.

lg.l: ——— Marullus lib. 1.dolor, querelae,

l.hi: Lamentatio, lachrymae perennes,
Languor, anxietas, amaritudo;
Aut si triste magis potest quid esse,

lg.l: Hos tu das Comites Neaera vitae.
[… pain, complaints,
Moaning, everlasting tears,
Weariness, anxiety, bitterness;
Or if there can be something harsher,
You bequeath these to me, Neaera, as my life’s companions.]

div.p: These be the companions of lovers, and the ordinary symptoms, as the Poet repeats them.

l.hi: In amore haec insunt vitia,
Suspitiones, inimicitiae, audaciae,

lg.l: Bellum, pax rursum, &c.

l.hi: Insomnia, aerumna, error, terror, & fuga,
Excogitantia, excors immodestia,
Petulantia, cupiditas, & malevolentia;
Inhaeret etiam aviditias, desidia, injuria,

lg.l: Inopia, contumelia & dispendium, &c.
In love these vices are; suspicions,
Peace, war, and impudence, detractions,
Dreams, cares, and errors, terrors and affrights,
Immodest pranks, devices, sleights and flights,
Heart-burnings, wants, neglects, desire of wrong,
Loss continual, expense and hurt among.

div.p: Every Poet is full of such catalogues of Love symptoms; but fear and sorrow may justly challenge the chief place. Though Hercules de Saxonia cap. 3 tract. de melanch. will exclude fear from Love-Melancholy, yet I am otherwise persuaded. Ovid.Res est solliciti plena timoris amor [Love’s a thing full of anxious fears]. ’Tis full of fear, anxiety, doubt, care, peevishness, suspicion, it turns a man into a woman, which made Hesiod belike, put fear and paleness Venus’ daughters,

lg.l: ——— Marti clypeos atque arma secanti

l.hi: Alma Venus peperit Pallorem, unaque Timorem:

lg.l: [… for Mars, cleaver of shields and arms,
Bountiful Venus bore Pallor, along with Fear:]

div.p: because fear and love are still linked together. Moreover they are apt to mistake, amplify, too credulous sometimes, too full of hope and confidence, and then again very jealous, unapt to believe or entertain any good news. The Comical Poet hath prettily painted out this passage amongst the rest in a Adelph. Act. 4 scen. 5.Dialogue betwixt Micio and Aeschinus, a gentle father and a lovesick son. M. Be of good cheer my son, thou shalt have her to wife. Ae. Ah father, do you mock me now? M. I mock thee, why? Ae. That which I so earnestly desire, I more suspect and fear. M. Get you home, and send for her to be your wife. Ae. What now a wife, now father, &c. These doubts, anxieties, suspicions, are the least part of their torments; they break many times from passions to actions, speak fair, and flatter, now most obsequious and willing, by and by they are averse, wrangle, fight, swear, quarrel, laugh, weep: and he that doth not so by fits, Tom. 4 dial. amorum.Lucian holds, is not thoroughly touched with this Loadstone of Love. So their actions and passions are intermixed, but of all other passions, Sorrow hath the greatest share; Aristotle 2 Rhet. puts love therefore in the irascible part. Ovid.Love to many is bitterness itself; rem amaram [an acrid thing] Plato calls it, a bitter potion, an agony, a plague.

l.hi: Eripite hanc pestem perniciemque mihi;
Quae mihi subrepens imos ut torpor in artus,

lg.l: Expulit ex omni pectore laetitias.
O take away this plague, this mischief from me,
Which as a numbness over all my body,
Expels my joys, and makes my soul so heavy.

div.p: Phaedria had a true touch of this, when he cried out,

lg.l: ——— Ter. Eunuch. Act. 1 sc. 2.O Thais, Utinam esset mihi

l.hi: Pars aequa amoris tecum, ac pariter fieret ut

lg.l: Aut hoc tibi doleret itidem, ut mihi dolet.
O Thais would thou hadst of these my pains a part,
Or as it doth me now, so it would make thee smart.

div.p: So had that young man, when he roared again for discontent,

l.hi: Jactor, crucior, agitor, stimulor,
Versor in amoris rota miser,
Exanimor, feror, distrahor, deripior,

lg.l: Ubi sum, ibi non sum; ubi non sum, ibi est animus.
I am vex’t and toss’d, and rack’t on Love’s wheel;
Where not, I am, but where am, do not feel.

div.p: The Moon in Tom. 3.Lucian, made her moan to Venus, that she was almost dead for love, pereo equidem amore [I’m truly dying for love], and after a long tale, she broke off abruptly and wept, Scis quod posthac dicturus fuerim [You know what I was going to say next].O Venus, thou knowest my poor heart. Charmides in Tom. 4 dial. meret.Lucian, was so impatient, that he sobbed and sighed, and tore his hair, and said he would hang himself, I am undone, O sister Tryphaena, I cannot endure these love pangs, what shall I do? Vos O dii Averrunci, solvite me his curis, O ye Gods, free me from these cares and miseries, out of the anguish of his Soul, Aristaenetus lib. 2 epist. 8.Theocles prays. Shall I say, most part of a Lover’s life is full of agony, anxiety, fear and grief, complaints, sighs, suspicions, and cares (heigh-ho, my heart is woe), full of silence and irksome solitariness?

l.hi: Frequenting shady bowers in discontent,

lg.l: To the air his fruitless clamours he will vent.

div.p: Except at such times that he hath lucida intervalla [lucid intervals], pleasant gales, or sudden alterations, as if his Mistress smile upon him, give him a good look, a kiss, or that some comfortable message be brought him, his service is accepted, &c.

He is then too confident and rapt beyond himself, as if he had heard the Nightingale in the Spring before the Cuckoo, or as Celestinae act. 1. Sancti majori laetitia non fruuntur. Si mihi deus omnium votorum mortalium summam concedat non magis, &c. [The saints do not enjoy a greater happiness. If God were to grant me the sum of all mortal wishes, {it would be} no greater, etc.]Calisto was at Melibea’s presence, Quis unquam hac mortali vita tam gloriosum corpus vidit? Humanitatem transcendere videor, &c., whoever saw so glorious a sight, what man ever enjoyed such delight? More content cannot be given of the Gods, wished,
had or hoped of any mortal man. There is no happiness in the world comparable to his, no content, no joy to this, no life to Love, he is in Paradise.

l.hi: Quis me uno vivit foelicior? Aut magis hac est
Optandum vita dicere quis poterit?

lg.l: Who lives so happy as myself? What bliss
In this our life may be compar’d to this?

div.p: He will not change fortune in that case with a Prince,

l.hi: Donec gratus eram tibi,

lg.l: Persarum vigui rege beatior.
[While I was beloved by you,
I bloomed, more blessed than the king of the Persians.]

div.p: The Persian Kings are not so jovial as he is, O Act. 3 scen. 5 Eunuch. Ter.festus dies hominis, O happy day; so Chaerea exclaims when he came from Pamphila his Sweetheart, well pleased,

foreign.hi: Nunc est profecto interfici cum perpeti me possem,
Ne hoc gaudium contaminet vita aliqua aegritudine,

div.p: he could find in his heart to be killed instantly, lest if he live longer, some sorrow or sickness should contaminate his joys. A little after, he was so merrily set upon the same occasion, that he could not contain himself.

foreign.hi: O populares, ecquis me vivit hodie fortunatior?
Nemo hercule quisquam; nam in me dii plane potestatem
Suam omnem ostendere;

div.p: is’t possible (O my Countrymen) for any living to be so happy as myself? No sure it cannot be, for the Gods have showed all their power, all their goodness in me. Yet by and by when this young Gallant was crossed in his wench, he laments, and cries, and roars downright.
I am undone,

lg.l: Neque virgo est usquam, neque ego, qui e conspectu illam amisi meo.

foreign.hi: Ubi quaeram, ubi investigem, quem percuncter, quam insistam viam?

div.p: The Virgin’s gone, and I am gone, she’s gone, she’s gone, and what shall I do? Where shall I seek her, where shall I find her, whom shall I ask? What way, what course shall I take? What will become of me?

lg.l: ——— Mantuan.vitales auras invitus agebat,

div.p: he was weary of his life, sick, mad and desperate, Ter. Adelph. 3. 4.utinam mihi esset aliquid hic, quo nunc me praecipitem darem [I wish there was something here for me now to throw myself off]. ’Tis not Chaerea’s case this alone, but his, and his, and every Lover’s in the like state. If he hear ill news, have bad success in his suit, she frown upon him, or that his Mistress in his presence respect another more (as Lib. 1 de contem. amoribus.Haedus observes), prefer another suitor, speak more familiarly to him, or use more kindly than himself, if by nod, smile, message she discloseth herself to another, he is instantly tormented, none so Love is a fiend, a fire, a heaven, a hell, where pleasure, pain, grief, and repentance dwell. R. T.dejected as he is, utterly undone, a castaway Calisto in Celestina.in quem fortuna omnia odiorum suorum crudelissima tela exonerat [on whom fortune discharges all the cruellest weapons of her hatred], a dead man, the scorn of fortune, a monster of fortune, worse than naught, the loss of a Kingdom had been less. Pornodidasc. dial. Ital.Aretine’s Lucretia made very good proof of this, as she relates it herself. For when I made some of my suitors believe I would betake myself to a Nunnery, they took on, as if they had lost Father and Mother, because they were forever after to want my company. Omnes labores leves fuere, all other labour was light; Ter.but this might not be endured,

lg.l: Tui carendum quod erat ———

div.p: for I cannot be without thy Company, mournful Amyntas, painful Amyntas, careful Amyntas; better a Metropolitan City were sacked, a Royal Army overcome, an invincible Armada sunk, and twenty thousand Kings should perish, than her little finger ache, so zealous are they, and so tender of her good. They would all turn Friars for my sake, as she follows it, in hope by that means to meet, or see me again, as my Confessors, at stool-ball, or at barley-break: and so afterwards when an importunate suitor came, if I had bid my Maid say that I was not at leisure, not within, busy, could not speak with him, he was instantly astonished, and stood like a pillar of marble; another went swearing, chafing, cursing, foaming.

lg.l: Mantuan.Illa sibi vox ipsa Jovis violentior ira, cum tonat, &c.
[For him that word was more savage than the wrath of Jove when he thunders, etc.]

div.p: The voice of a mandrake had been sweeter music; but he to whom I gave entertainment, was in the Elysian fields, ravished for joy, quite beyond himself. ’Tis the general humour of all Lovers, she is their stern, Pole star, and guide.

lg.l: Leochaeus.Deliciumque animi, deliquiumque sui.
[Both the delight of their soul and their own eclipse.]

div.p: As a Tulipant to the Sun (which our Herbalists call Narcissus) when it shines, is admirandus flos ad radios solis se pandens, a glorious Flower exposing itself; but when the Sun sets, or a tempest comes, it hides itself, pines away, and hath no pleasure left (which Carolus Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, in a cause not unlike, sometimes used for an Impress), do all inamorates to their Mistress, she is their Sun, their Primum mobile, or anima informans; this Emblem. amat. 33.one hath elegantly expressed by a windmill, still moved by the wind, which otherwise hath no motion of itself.

lg.l: Sic tua ni spiret gratia, truncus ero.
[So, unless your love inspires me, I’ll be a stump.]

div.p: He is wholly animated from her breath, his soul lives in her body, Calisto de Melibea.sola claves habet interitus & salutis, she keeps the keys of his life; his fortune ebbs and flows with her favour, a gracious or bad aspect turns him up or down,

lg.l: Mens mea lucescit Lucia luce tua.
[My heart begins to shine, Lucia, with your light.]

div.p: Howsoever his present state be pleasing or displeasing, ’tis continuate so long as he loves, he can do nothing, think of nothing but her; desire hath no rest, she is his Cynosure, Hesperus & Vesper, his morning and evening Star, his Goddess, his Mistress, Anima non est ubi animat, sed ubi amat [The soul exists not where it gives life, but where it loves].his life, his soul, his everything, dreaming, waking, she is always in his mouth; his heart, eyes, ears, and all his thoughts are full of her. His Laura, his Victorina, his Columbina, Flavia, Flaminia, Caelia, Delia or Isabella (call her how you will), she is the sole object of his senses, the substance of his soul, nidulus animae suae [the little nest of his soul], he magnifies her above measure, totus in illa, full of her, can breathe nothing but her. I adore Melibea, saith Lovesick Celestine act. 1.Calisto, I believe in Melibea, I honour, admire and love my Melibea; his soul was soused, imparadised, imprisoned in his Lady. When Ter. Eunuch. Act. 1 sc. 2.Thais took her leave of Phaedria,

lg.l: ——— mi Phaedria, & nunquid aliud vis?

div.p: Sweetheart (she said) will you command me any further service? He readily replied, and gave this in charge,

lg.l: ——— egone quid velim?

l.hi: Dies noctesque ames me, me desideres,
Me somnies, me expectes, me cogites,
Me speres, me te oblectes, mecum tota sis,

lg.l: Meus fac postremo animus, quando ego sum tuus.
Dost ask (my dear) what service I will have?
To love me day and night is all I crave,
To dream on me, to expect, to think on me,
Depend and hope, still covet me to see,
Delight thyself in me, be wholly mine,
For know my love, that I am wholly thine.

div.p: But all this needed not, you will say, if she affect once, she will be his, settle her love on him, on him alone,

lg.l: ——— Virg. 4 Aen.illum absens absentem
Auditque videtque ———
[… she, absent, both hears and sees
That absent man …]

div.p: she can, she must think and dream of naught else but him, continually of him, as did Orpheus on his Eurydice,

l.hi: Te dulcis conjux, te solo in littore mecum,

lg.l: Te veniente die, te discedente canebam.
On thee sweet wife was all my song,
Morn, Evening, and all along.

div.p: And Dido upon her Aeneas;

lg.l: ——— & quae me insomnia terrent,
Multa viri virtus, & plurima currit Imago.
[‘… and what dreams terrify me!’
Often the hero’s bravery, and very often his image, appear in her mind.]
And ever and anon, she thinks upon the man
That was so fine, so fair, so blithe, so debonair.

div.p: Clitophon in the first book of Achilles Tatius, complaineth how that his Mistress Leucippe tormented him much more in the night, than in the day. For all day long he had some object or other to distract his senses, but in the night all ran upon her: all night long he lay Tota hac nocte somnum hisce oculis non vidi [My eyes didn’t get a wink of sleep last night]. Ter.awake and could think of nothing else but her, he could not get her out of his mind, towards morning sleep took a little pity on him, he slumbered a while, but all his dreams were of her.

lg.l: ——— Buchanan. Sylv.te nocte sub atra

l.hi: Alloquor, amplector, falsaque in imagine somni,

lg.l: Gaudia solicitam palpant evanida mentem.
In the dark night I speak, embrace and find,
That fading joys deceive my careful mind.

div.p: The same complaint Euryalus makes to his Lucretia, Aeneas Silvius.day and night I think of thee, I wish for thee, I talk of thee, call on thee, look for thee, hope for thee, delight myself in thee, day and night I love thee.

l.hi: Nec mihi vespero
Surgente decedunt amores,
Nec rapidum fugiente solem;

lg.l: [My love does not subside
When the evening star is rising,
Or when it’s fleeing the onrushing sun;]

div.p: Morning, Evening, all is alike with me, I have restless thoughts,

lg.l: Petronius.Te vigilans oculis, animo te nocte requiro.
[Awake, I seek you with my eyes; at night, with my mind.]

div.p: Still I think on thee. Anima non est ubi animat, sed ubi amat [The soul exists not where it gives life, but where it loves]. I live and breathe in thee, I wish for thee.

l.hi: O niveam quae te poterit mihi reddere lucem,

lg.l: O mihi felicem terque quaterque diem.
[O snow-bright dawn, that can return you to me,
O lucky day for me, three, four times over!]

div.p: O happy day that shall restore thee to my sight. In the meantime he raves on her; her sweet face, eyes, actions, gestures, hands, feet, speech, length, breadth, height, depth, and the rest of her dimensions, are so surveyed, measured, and taken, by that Astrolabe of fantasy, and that so violently sometimes, with such earnestness and eagerness, such continuance, so strong an imagination, that at length he thinks he sees her indeed; he talks with her, he embraceth her, Ixion-like pro Junone nubem, a cloud for Juno, as he said. Nihil praeter Leucippen cerno, Leucippe mihi perpetuo in oculis, & animo versatur, I see and meditate of naught but Leucippe. Be she present or absent, all is one;

l.hi: Et quamvis aberat placidae praesentia formae,

lg.l: Quem dederat praesens forma, manebat amor.
[And although the presence of that pleasing beauty was absent,
The love, to which its presence had given form, remained.]

div.p: That impression of her beauty is still fixed in his mind,

lg.l: ——— Virg. Aen. 4.haerent infixi pectore vultus,
[… the imprinted features stick fast in the heart,]

div.p: as he that is bitten with a mad dog, thinks all he sees dogs, dogs in his meat, dogs in his dish, dogs in his drink: his mistress is in his eyes, ears, heart, in all his senses. Valleriola had a merchant his patient in the same predicament: and De Pythonicis.Ulricus Molitor out of Austin, hath a story of one, that through vehemency of his love passion, still thought he saw his Mistress present with him, she talked with him, et commisceri cum ea vigilans videbatur [and when awake he seemed to be having intercourse with her], still embracing him.

Now if this passion of love can produce such effects, if it be pleasantly intended, what bitter torments shall it breed, when it is with fear and continual sorrow, suspicion, care, agony, as commonly it is, still accompanied, what an intolerable Juno, nec ira deum tantum nec tela, nec hostis, quantum tute noces animis illapsus [Juno, neither the anger of the gods, nor the spear, nor the enemy, are as hurtful as you when you have flowed into our souls]. Silius Ital. 15 bel. Punic. de amore.pain must it be?

lg.l: ——— Non tam grandes

l.hi: Gargara culmos, quot demerso
Pectore curas longa nexas
Usque catena, vel quae penitus

lg.l: Crudelis amor vulnera miscet.
Mount Gargarus hath not so many stems,
As Lover’s breast hath grievous wounds,
And linked cares, which love compounds.

div.p: When the King of Babylon would have punished a Courtier of his, for loving a young Lady of the royal blood, and far above his fortunes, Philostratus vita ejus.Apollonius in presence, by all means persuaded him to let him alone; for to love and not enjoy was a most unspeakable torment, no tyrant could invent the like punishment; as a gnat at a candle, in a short space he would consume himself. For Love is a perpetual Ausonius cap. 35.flux, angor animi [a torment of the mind], a warfare, militat omnis amans [every lover wages war], a grievous wound is love still, and a Lover’s heart is Cupid’s quiver, a consuming Et caeco carpitur igne; & mihi sese offert ultro meus ignis Amyntas [But he is consumed by a secret fire; and my flame Amyntas offers himself to me without being asked].fire, Ter. Eunuch.accede ad hanc ignem, &c. [come closer to this flame, etc.], an inextinguible fire.

lg.l: ——— Seneca Hippol.alitur & crescit malum,

l.hi: Et ardet intus, qualis Aetnaeo vapor

lg.l: Exundat antro ———
[… My torment feeds and grows,
And burns inside, like the steam
That flows from the crater of Etna …]

div.p: as Etna rageth, so doth Love, and more than Etna or any material fire.

lg.l: ——— Theocritus idyl. 2. Levibus cor est violabile telis [The heart is easily wounded by light missiles].Nam amor saepe Lypareo
Vulcano ardentiorem flammam incendere solet.
[… For love often burns hotter
Than the flame of Liparian Vulcan.]

div.p: Vulcan’s flames are but smoke to this; for fire, saith Xenophon, burns them alone that stand near it, or touch it; but this fire of Love burneth and scorcheth afar off, and is more hot and vehement than any material fire; Nonius.Ignis in igne furit, ’tis a fire in a fire, the quintessence of fire. For when Nero burnt Rome, as Calisto urgeth, he fired houses, consumed men’s bodies and goods; but this fire devours the soul itself, and one soul is worth 100,000 bodies. No water can quench this wild-fire.

lg.l: ——— Mant. ecl. 2.In pectus caecos absorbuit ignes,

l.hi: Ignes qui nec aqua perimi potuere, nec imbre

lg.l: Diminui, neque graminibus, magicisque susurris.
A fire he took into his breast,
Which water could not quench,
Nor herb, nor art, nor Magic spells
Could quell, nor any drench.

div.p: Except it be tears and sighs, for so they may chance find a little ease.

l.hi: Sic candentia colla, sic patens frons,
Sic me blanda tui, Neaera, ocelli,
Sic pares minio genae perurunt,
Ut ni me lachrymae rigent perennes,

lg.l: Totus in tenues eam favillas.
So thy white neck Neaera me poor soul
Doth scorch, thy cheeks, thy wanton eyes that roll:
Were it not for my dropping tears that hinder,
I should be quite burnt up forthwith to cinder.

div.p: This fire strikes like lightning, Imagines deorum.which made those old Grecians paint Cupid in many of their Temples with Jupiter’s thunderbolts in his hands; for it wounds, and cannot be perceived how, whence it came, where it pierced,

l.hi: Urimur, & caecum pectora vulnus habent,

lg.l: [We burn, and our feelings bear the hidden wound,]

div.p: and can hardly be discerned at first.

lg.l: ——— Aeneid. 4.Est mollis flamma medullas,
Et tacitum insano vivit sub pectore vulnus.
A gentle wound, an easy fire it was,
And sly at first, and secretly did pass.

div.p: But by and by it began to range and burn amain;

lg.l: ——— Seneca.Pectus insanum vapor,

l.hi: Amorque torret, intus saevus vorat
Penitus medullas, atque per venas meat
Visceribus ignis mersus, & venis latens,

lg.l: Ut agilis altas flamma percurrit trabes.
This fiery vapour rageth in the veins,
And scorcheth entrails, as when fire burns
An house, it nimbly runs along the beams,
And at last the whole it overturns.

div.p: Abraham Hosemannus lib. 1 amor. conjugal. cap. 2 pag. 22 relates out of Plato, how that Empedocles the Philosopher was present at the cutting up of one that died for love, his heart was combust, his liver smoky, his lungs dried up, insomuch that he verily believed his soul was either sod or roasted, through the vehemency of love’s fire. Which belike made a modern writer of amorous Emblems, express Love’s fury by a pot hanging over the fire, and Cupid blowing the coals. As the heat consumes the water,

foreign.hi: Sic sua consumit viscera caecus amor,

div.p: so doth Love dry up his radical moisture. Another compares Love to a melting torch, which stood too near the fire.

l.hi: Sic quo quis propior suae puellae est,

lg.l: Hoc stultus propior suae ruinae est.
The nearer he unto his mistress is,
The nearer he unto his ruin is.

div.p: So that to say truth, as Lib. 4.Castilio describes it, The beginning, middle, end of Love is naught else but sorrow, vexation, agony, torment, irksomeness, wearisomeness, so that to be squalid, ugly, miserable, solitary, discontent, dejected, to wish for death, to complain, rave, and to be peevish, are the certain signs, and ordinary actions of a lovesick person. This continual pain and torture makes them forget themselves, if they be far gone with it, in doubt, despair of obtaining, or eagerly bent, to neglect all ordinary business.

lg.l: ——— Virg. Aen. 4.pendent opera interrupta, minaeque
Murorum ingentes, aequataque machina coelo.
[… The interrupted works are left hanging,
The huge menacing walls, and the sky-reaching cranes.]

div.p: Lovesick Dido left her works undone, so did Seneca Hipp. act. 1.Phaedra,

lg.l: ——— Palladis telae vacant,
Et inter ipsas pensa labuntur manus.
[… the loom of Athena stands idle,
And the wool slips between my very hands.]

div.p: Faustus in Ecl. 1.Mantuan, took no pleasure in anything he did,

l.hi: Nulla quies mihi dulcis erat, nullus labor aegro
Pectore, sensus iners, & mens torpore sepulta,

lg.l: Carminis occiderat studium. ———
[No rest, no work was sweet to me. In my heart’s sickness
The senses were numb, and the mind buried in torpor;
It had murdered my love of singing …]

div.p: And ’tis the humour of them all, to be careless of their persons, and their estates, as the shepherd in Idyl. 14.Theocritus, et haec barba inculta est, squalidique capilli [this beard’s a mess, and the hair’s filthy], their beards flag, and they have no more care of pranking themselves or of any business, they care not as they say, which end goes forward.

l.hi: Oblitusque greges, & rura domestica totus

lg.l: Ovid. Met. 13 de Polyphemo: Uritur oblitus pecorum, antrorumque suorum, Jamque tibi formae, &c. [on Polyphemus: he burns, forgetful of his flocks and caves; and now {Polyphemus, you care about} your appearance, etc.]Uritur & noctes in luctum expendit amaras.
Forgetting flocks of sleep and country farms,
The silly shepherd always mourns and burns.

div.p: Lovesick Ter. Eunuch.Chaerea when he came from Pamphila’s house, and had not so good welcome as he did expect, was all amort, Parmeno meets him, quid tristis es? Why art thou so sad man? Unde es? Whence comest, how dost? But he sadly replies, Ego hercle nescio neque unde eam, neque quorsum eam, ita prorsus oblitus sum mei, I have so forgotten myself, I neither know where I am, nor whence I come, nor whether I will, what I do. P. How so? Ch. I am in love.

lg.l: ——— Ter. Eunuch.Prudens sciens
vivus vidensque pereo, nec quid agam scio.
[… In full awareness and knowledge,
alive and alert, I’m dying, and I don’t know what to do.]

div.p: He that erst had his thoughts free (as Philostratus Lemnius in an Epistle of his, describes this fiery passion) and spent his time like an hard student, in those delightsome philosophical precepts, he that with the Sun and Moon wandered all over the world, with Stars themselves ranged about, and left no secret or small mystery in Nature unsearched, since he was enamoured, can do nothing now but think and meditate of love matters, day and night composeth himself how to please his Mistress; all his study, endeavour, is to approve himself to his Mistress, to win his Mistress’ favour, to compass his desire, to be counted her servant. When Peter Abelardus that great Scholar of his age,

l.note: Pars Epitaphii ejus [Part of his epitaph].
l.hi: Cui soli patuit scibile quicquid erat,

lg.l: [To whom, alone, all that was knowable was revealed,]

div.p: was now in love with Heloissa, he had no mind to visit or frequent Schools and Scholars any more. Taediosum mihi valde fuit (as Epist. prima.he confesseth) ad scholas procedere, vel in iis morari [It was very irksome for me … to go to the schools, or to stay in them], all his mind was on his new Mistress.

Now to this end and purpose, if there be any hope of obtaining his suit, to prosecute his cause, he will spend himself, goods, fortunes for her, and though he lose and alienate all his friends, be threatened, be cast off, and disinherited; for as the Poet saith, Boethius, lib. 3 Met. ult.Amori quis legem det? [who can legislate for love?] Though he be utterly undone by it, disgraced, go a-begging, yet for her sweet sake, to enjoy her, he will willingly beg, hazard all he hath, goods, lands, shame, scandal, fame, and life itself.

l.hi: Non recedam neque quiescam, noctu & interdiu,

lg.l: Prius profecto quam aut ipsam, aut mortem investigavero.
I’ll never rest or cease my suit,
Till she or death do make me mute.

div.p:
Parthenis in Epist. lib. 6.Aristaenetus was fully resolved to do as much. I may have better matches I confess, but farewell shame, farewell honour, farewell honesty, farewell friends and fortunes, &c. O Harpedone keep my counsel, I will leave all for his sweet sake, I will have him, say no more, contra gentes [against the world], I am resolved, I will have him. Theodor. Prodromus lib. 3 Amor.Gobryas the Captain, when he had
espied Rhodanthe, the fair captive Maid, fell upon his knees before Mistylus the General, with tears, vows, and all the Rhetoric he could, by the scars he had formerly received, the good service he had done, or whatsoever else was dear unto him, besought his Governor he might have the captive Virgin to be his wife, virtutis suae spolium, as a reward of his worth and service; and moreover, he would forgive him the money which was owing, and all reckonings besides due unto him, I ask no more, no part of booty, no portion, but Rhodanthe to be my wife. And when as he could not compass her by fair means, he fell to treachery, force and villainy, and set his life at stake at last, to accomplish his desire. ’Tis a common humour this, a general passion of all Lovers to be so affected, and which Emilia told Aretine a Courtier in Castilio’s discourse, Lib. 2.surely Aretine, if thou werst not so indeed, thou didst not love; ingenuously confess, for if thou hadst been thoroughly enamoured, thou wouldst have desired nothing more than to please thy Mistress. For that is the law of love, to will and nill the same,

lg.l: Stroza fil. Epig.Tantum velle & nolle, velit nolit quod amica.

div.p: Undoubtedly this may be pronounced of them all, they are very slaves, drudges for the time, madmen, fools, dizzards, Quippe haec omnia ex atra bile & amore proveniunt [In fact all these things are produced by black bile and love]. Jason Pratensis.atrabilarii [melancholics], beside themselves, and as blind as Beetles. Their Immensus amor ipsa stultitia est [Boundless love is stupidity itself], Cardan. lib. 2 de sapientia.dotage is most eminent, Amare simul & sapere ipsi Jovi non datur, as Seneca holds, Jupiter himself cannot love and be wise both together; the very best of them, if once they be overtaken with this passion, the most staid, discreet, grave, generous and wise, otherwise able to govern themselves, in this commit many absurdities, many indecorums, unbefitting their gravity and persons.

l.hi: Quisquis amat servit, sequitur captivus amantem,

lg.l: Fert domita cervice jugum ———
[Whoever loves is a slave; he follows his beloved as a captive,
He bears the yoke with a tamed neck …]

div.p: Samson, David, Solomon, Hercules, Socrates, &c., are justly taxed of indiscretion in this point; the middle sort are betwixt hawk and buzzard; and although they do perceive and acknowledge their own dotage, weakness, fury, yet they cannot withstand it; as well may witness those expostulations, and confessions of Dido in Virgil,

lg.l: Virg. Aen. 4.Incipit effari mediaque in voce resistit.
[She starts to speak, and stops mid-flow.]

div.p: Phaedra in Seneca,

l.hi: Quod ratio poscit, vincit ac regnat furor,

lg.l: Potensque tota mente dominatur deus.
[What reason asks for, passion conquers and rules,
And dominates the whole soul as a mighty god.]

div.p: Myrrha in Met. 10.Ovid,

l.hi: Illa quidem sentit, foedoque repugnat amori,
Et secum quo mente feror, quid molior, inquit,

lg.l: Dii precor, & pietas, &c.
She sees and knows her fault, and doth resist,
Against her filthy lust she doth contend,
And whither go I, what am I about?
And God forbid, yet doth it in the end.

div.p: Again,

lg.l: ——— Pervigil igne,

l.hi: Carpitur indomito, furiosaque vota retrectat,
Et modo desperat, modo vult tentare, pudetque

lg.l: Et cupit, & quid agat, non invenit, &c.
With raging lust she burns, and now recalls
Her vow, and then despairs, and when ’tis past,
Her former thoughts she’ll prosecute in haste,
And what to do she knows not at the last.

div.p: She will and will not, abhors; and yet as Medea did, doth it,

lg.l: ——— Trahit invitam nova vis, aliudque cupido,

l.hi: Mens aliud suadet, video meliora, proboque,

lg.l: Deteriora sequor. ———
Reason pulls one way, burning lust another,
She sees and knows what’s good, but she doth neither.

l.hi: O fraus, amorque, & mentis emotae furor,
Quo me abstulistis?

lg.l: [O delusion, love and fury of an unhinged mind,
Where have you taken me?]

div.p:
The major part of Lovers are carried headlong like so many brute beasts, reason counsels one way, their friends, fortunes, shame, disgrace, danger, and an ocean of cares that will certainly follow; yet this furious lust, precipitates, counterpoiseth, weighs down on the other; though it be their utter undoing, perpetual infamy, loss, yet they will do it, and become at last insensati void of sense; degenerate into dogs, hogs, asses, brutes; as Jupiter into a Bull, Apuleius
an Ass, Lycaon a wolf, Tereus a Lapwing, An immodest woman is like a Bear.Callisto a Bear, Elpenor and Gryllus into Swine by Circe. For what else may we think those ingenious Poets to have shadowed in their witty fictions and poems, but that a man once given over to his lust (as Feram induit dum rosas comedat, i. dum ad se redeat [He assumes the part of a wild beast until he eats the roses, that is, until he recovers his senses].Fulgentius interprets that of Apuleius, Alciatus of Tereus) is no better than a beast.

l.note: Alciatus de upupa Embl. Animal immundum upupa stercora amans, ave hac nihil foedius, nihil libidinosius [The hoopoe is a filthy animal, loving ordure; nothing’s more repulsive, nothing’s more lustful than this bird]. Sabin. in Ovid. Met.
l.hi: Rex fueram, sic crista docet, sed sordida vita

lg.l: Immundam e tanto culmine fecit avem.
I was a King, my Crown a witness is,
But by my filthiness am come to this.

div.p: Their blindness is all out as great, as manifest as their weakness and dotage, or rather an inseparable companion, an ordinary sign of it. Love is like a false glass which represents everything fairer than it is.Love is blind, as the saying is, Cupid’s blind, and so are all his followers.

lg.l: Quisquis amat ranam, ranam putat esse Dianam.
[Whoever loves a frog, thinks the frog is Diana.]

div.p:
Every Lover admires his Mistress, though she be very deformed of herself, ill-favoured, wrinkled, pimpled, pale, red, yellow, tanned, tallow-faced, have a swollen Juggler’s platter face, or a thin, lean, chitty face, have clouds in her face, be crooked, dry, bald, goggle-eyed, blear-eyed or with staring eyes, she looks like a squized cat, hold her head still awry, heavy, dull, hollow-eyed, black or yellow about the eyes, or squint-eyed, sparrow-mouthed, Persian hook-nosed, have sharp Fox nose, a red nose, China flat, great nose, nare simo patuloque [wide- and snub-nosed], a nose like a promontory, gubber-tushed, rotten teeth, black, uneven, brown teeth, beetle-browed, a Witch’s beard, her breath stink all over the room, her nose drop winter and summer, with a Bavarian poke under her chin, a sharp chin, lave-eared, with a long crane’s neck, which stands awry too, pendulis mammis [with drooping breasts], her dugs like two double jugs, or else no dugs, in that other extreme, bloody-fallen fingers, she have filthy long unpared nails, scabbed hands or wrists, a tanned skin, a rotten carcass, crooked back, she stoops, is lame, splay-footed, as slender in the middle as a cow in the waist, gouty legs, her ankles hang over her shoes, her feet stink, she breed lice, a mere changeling, a very monster, an aufe imperfect, her whole complexion savours, an harsh voice, incondite gesture, vile gait, a vast virago, or an ugly tit, a slug, a fat fustilugs, a truss, a long lean raw-bone, a skeleton, a sneaker (si qua latent meliora puta [you imagine whatever’s hidden to be more beautiful]), and to thy judgement looks like a mard in a lantern, whom thou couldst not fancy for a world, but hatest, loathest, and wouldst have spit in her face, or blow thy nose in her bosom, remedium amoris [an antidote for love] to another man, a dowdy, a slut, a scold, a nasty, rank, rammy, filthy, beastly quean, dishonest peradventure,
obscene, base, beggarly, rude, foolish, untaught, peevish, Irus’ daughter, Thersites’ sister, Grobian’s scholar, if he love her once, he admires her for all this, he takes no notice of any such errors, or imperfections of body or mind.

lg.l: ——— Hor. ser. lib. 1 Sat. 3.Ipsa haec

l.hi: delectant, veluti Balbinum Polypus Agnae,

lg.l: [… These very things
delight him, like Balbinus with Hagna’s polyp,]

div.p: he had rather have her than any woman in the world. If he were a King, she alone should be his Queen, his Empress. O that he had but the wealth and treasure of both the Indies to endow her with, a carrack of Diamonds, a chain of Pearl, a caskanet of Jewels (a pair of calf-skin gloves of fourpence a pair were fitter) or some such toy, to send her for a token, she should have it with all his heart; he would spend myriads of crowns for her sake. Venus herself, Panthea, Cleopatra, Tarquin’s Tanaquil, Herod’s Mariamne, or The daughter and heir of Carolus Pugnax.Mary of Burgundy if she were alive, would not match her.

lg.l: (Seneca in Octavia.Vincet vultus haec Tyndaridos,
Qui moverunt horrida bella.
[This one here will surpass the face of Helen,
Which inspired terrible war.]

div.p: Let Paris himself be judge) renowned Helena comes short, that Rodopheian Phyllis, Larissean Coronis, Babylonian Thisbe, Polyxena, Laura, Lesbia, &c., your counterfeit Ladies were never so fair as she is.

l.hi: Quicquid erit placidi, lepidi, grati, atque faceti,

lg.l: Vivida cunctorum retines Pandora deorum,
Whate’er is pretty, pleasant, facete, well,
Whate’er Pandora had, she doth excel.
Mantuan. Ecl. 1.Dicebam Triviae formam nihil esse Dianae.
[I used to say that the beauty of Diana Trivia was nothing.]

div.p: Diana was not to be compared to her, nor Juno, nor Minerva, nor any Goddess. Thetis’ feet were as bright as silver, the ankles of Hebe clearer than Crystal, the arms of Aurora as ruddy as the Rose, Juno’s breasts as white as snow, Minerva wise, Venus fair; but what of this? Dainty come thou to me. She is all in all,

lg.l: ——— Angerianus.Caelia ridens
Est Venus, incedens Juno, Minerva loquens.
[… laughing, Caelia is Venus;
Walking, she’s Juno; talking, she’s Minerva.]
Faerie Queene Cant. 2 lib. 4.Fairest of fair, that fairness doth excel.

div.p: Euhemerus in Aristaenetus, so far admireth his good Mistress’ good parts, that he makes proclamation of them, and challengeth all comers in her behalf. Epist. 12.Whoever saw the beauties of the East, or of the West, let them come from all quarters, all, and tell truth, if ever they saw such an excellent feature as this is. A goodfellow in Petronius cries out, no tongue can tell his Lady’s fine feature, or express it, quicquid dixeris minus erit, &c. [whatever you say will be inadequate, etc.]

lg.l: No tongue can her perfections tell,
In whose each part, all tongues may dwell.

div.p: Most of your lovers are of his humour and opinion. She is nulli secunda [second to none], a rare creature, a Phoenix, the sole commandress of his thoughts, Queen of his desires, his only delight: as Calcagnini dial. Galat.Triton now feelingly sings, that Lovesick Sea-God.

l.hi: Candida Leucothoe placet, & placet atra Melaene,

lg.l: Sed Galatea placet longe magis omnibus una.
Fair Leucothoe, black Melaene please me well,
But Galatea doth by odds the rest excel.

div.p: All the gracious Elogies, Metaphors, Hyperbolical comparisons of the best things in the world, the most glorious names; whatsoever, I say, is pleasant, amiable, sweet, grateful, and delicious, are too little for her.

lg.l: Phoebo pulchrior & sorore Phoebi.
His Phoebe is so fair, she is so bright,
She dims the Sun’s lustre, and the Moon’s light.

div.p: Stars, Suns, Moons, Metals, sweet-smelling Flowers, Odours, perfumes, Colours, Gold, Silver, Ivory, Pearls, Precious Stones, Snow, painted Birds, Doves, Honey, Sugar, Spice, cannot express her, Catullus.so soft, so tender, so radiant, sweet, so fair is she.

lg.l: ——— Mollior cuniculi capillo, &c.
[… Softer than rabbit’s fur, etc.]

foreign.hi: Lydia bella, puella candida,
Quae bene superas lac, & lilium,
Albamque simul rosam & rubicundam,

lg.l: Et expolitum ebur Indicum.
Fine Lydia my Mistress white and fair,
The milk, the Lily do not thee come near;
The Rose so white, the Rose so red to see,
And Indian Ivory comes short of thee:

div.p: such a description our English Homer makes of a fair Lady.

foreign.hi: That Emilia that was fairer to seen,
Than is Lily upon the stalk green:
And fresher than May with flowers new,
For with the Rose colour strove her hue,
I not which was the fairer of the two.

div.p: In this very phrase Ovid. Met. 13.Polyphemus courts Galatea.

l.hi: Candidior folio nivei Galatea ligustri,
Floridior prato, longa procerior alno,

lg.l: Splendidior vitro, tenero lascivior haedo, &c.
Mollior & cigni plumis, & lacte coacto.
Whiter Galat than the white withywind
Fresher than a field, higher than a tree,
Brighter than glass, more wanton than a Kid,
Softer than Swan’s down, or aught that may be.

div.p: So she admires him again, in that conceited Dialogue of Lucian, which John Secundus, an Elegant Dutch modern Poet hath translated into verse. When Doris and those other Sea-Nymphs, upbraided her with her ugly misshapen Lover Polyphemus; she replies, they speak out of envy and malice,

l.hi: Et plane invidia huc mera vos stimulare videtur,
Quod non vos itidem ut me Polyphemus amet;

lg.l: [And clearly it’s pure jealousy that spurs you on,
Because Polyphemus doesn’t love you as he does me;]

div.p: say what they could, he was a proper man. And as Heloissa writ to her Sweetheart Peter Abelardus, Si me Augustus orbis imperator uxorem expeteret, mallem tua esse meretrix quam orbis imperatrix; [if Augustus, the emperor of the world, wanted to marry me,] she had rather be his vassal, his Quean, than the world’s Empress or Queen.

lg.l: ——— non si me Jupiter ipse forte velit, ———
[… Not even if Jupiter himself should come to want me …]

div.p: she would not change her love for Jupiter himself.

To thy thinking she is a most loathsome creature; and as when a country fellow discommended once that exquisite Picture of Helena, made by Zeuxis, Plutarch.for he saw no such beauty in it; Nicomachus a lovesick spectator replied,
Sume tibi meos oculos & deam existimabis, take mine eyes, and thou wilt think she is a Goddess, dote on her forthwith, count all her vices, virtues; her imperfections, infirmities, absolute and perfect. If she be flat-nosed, she is lovely; if hook-nosed, kingly; if dwarfish and little, pretty; if tall, proper and manly, our brave British Bunduica; if crooked, wise; if monstrous, comely; her defects are no defects at all, she hath no deformities. Immo nec ipsum amicae stercus foetat [No indeed: even his girlfriend’s dung doesn’t stink], though she be nasty, fulsome, as Sostrata’s bitch, or Parmeno’s sow: thou hadst as lief have a snake in thy bosom, a toad in thy dish, and callest her witch, devil, hag, with all the filthy names thou canst invent; he admires her on the other side, she is his Idol, Lady, Mistress, Venerilla, Queen, the quintessence of beauty, an Angel, a Quanto quam Lucifer, aurea Phoebe, Tanto virginibus conspectior omnibus Herce [As the golden moon outshines the morning star, so is Herse fairer than all the virgins], Ovid.Star, a Goddess.

l.hi: Thou art my Vesta, thou my Goddess art,

lg.l: Thy hallowed Temple only is my heart.

div.p: The fragrancy of a thousand Courtesans is in her face: nec pulchrae effigies haec Cypridis aut Stratonices [nor those beautiful images of Venus or Stratonice], ’tis not Venus’ picture that, nor the Spanish Infanta’s as you suppose (good Sir), no Princess, or King’s daughter; no, no, but his divine Mistress forsooth, his dainty Dulcinea, his dear Antiphila, to whose service he is wholly consecrate, whom he alone adores.

l.hi: Cui comparatus indecens erit pavo,

lg.l: Inamabilis sciurus, & frequens Phoenix.
To whom confer’d a Peacock’s undecent,
A Squirrel’s harsh, a Phoenix too frequent.

div.p: All the graces, Veneres, elegances, pleasures, attend her. He prefers her before a Myriad of Court Ladies.

l.hi: He that commends Phyllis or Neaera,
Or Amaryllis, or Galatea,
Tityrus or Melibea, by your leave,

lg.l: Let him be mute, his Love the praises have.

div.p: Nay, before all the Gods and Goddesses themselves. So Tully. lib. 1 de nat. deor.Quintus Catulus admired his squint-eyed friend Roscius.

lg.l: Pace mihi liceat (Caelestes) dicere vestra,
Mortalis visus pulchrior esse Deo.
By your leave gentle Gods, this I’ll say true,
There’s none of you that have so fair an hue.

div.p: All the bombast Epithets, pathetical adjuncts, incomparably fair, curiously neat, divine, sweet, dainty, delicious, &c., pretty diminutives, corculum, suaviolum, &c. [little heart, little kiss, etc.], pleasant names may be invented, bird, mouse, lamb, puss, pigeon, pigsney, Kid, honey, love, dove, chicken, duck, &c., he puts on her.

l.hi: Meum mel, mea suavitas, meum cor,
Meum suaviolum, mei lepores,

lg.l: [My honey, my lovely, my heart,
My little kiss, my sweets,]

div.p: my life, my light, my jewel, my glory, Barthius.Margareta speciosa, cujus respectu omnia mundi pretiosa sordent [beautiful Margaret, all the riches of the world seem worthless compared to her], my sweet Margaret, my sole delight and darling. And as Ariosto, lib. 29 hist. 8.Rodomont courted Isabella;

l.hi: By all kind words, and gestures that he might,
He calls her his dear heart, his sole beloved,

lg.l: His joyful comfort, and his sweet delight.

l.hi: His Mistress, and his Goddess, and such names,

lg.l: As loving Knights apply to lovely Dames.

div.p: Every cloth she wears, every fashion pleaseth him above measure; her hand,

l.hi: O quales digitos, quas habet illa manus!

lg.l: [Oh, such fingers, what a hand she has!]

div.p: pretty foot, pretty coronets, her sweet carriage, sweet voice, tone, O that pretty tone, her divine and lovely looks, her everything, lovely sweet, amiable and pretty, pretty, pretty. Her very name (let it be what it will) is a most pretty pleasing name; I believe now there is some secret power and virtue in names, every action, sight, habit, gesture; he admires, whether she play, sing, or dance, in what tires soever she goeth, how excellent it was, how well it became her, never the like seen or heard.

lg.l: Tibullus.Mille habet ornatus, mille decenter habet.
[She has a thousand costumes, and wears a thousand gracefully.]

div.p: Let her wear what she will, do what she will, say what she will,

lg.l: Marull. lib. 2.Quicquid enim dicit, seu facit, omne decet.

div.p: He applauds and admires everything she wears, saith or doth,

l.hi: Illam quicquid agit, quoquo vestigia vertit,
Composuit furtim subsequiturque decor;
Seu solvit crines, fusis decet esse capillis,

lg.l: Seu compsit, comptis est reverenda comis.
Whate’er she doth, or whither e’er she go,
A sweet and pleasing grace attends forsooth;
Or loose, or bind her hair, or comb it up,
She’s to be honoured in what she doth.

div.p: Aristaenetus Epist. 1.Vestem induitur, formosa est, exuitur, tota forma est, let her be dressed or undressed, all is one, she is excellent still, beautiful, fair, and lovely to be behold. Women do as much by men; nay more, far fonder, weaker, and that by many parasangs. Come to me my dear Lysias (saith Musarium in Epist. 24.Aristaenetus), come quickly Sweetheart, all other men are Satyrs, mere clowns, blockheads to thee, nobody to thee: thy looks, words, gestures, actions, &c., are incomparably beyond all others. Venus was never so much besotted on her Adonis, Phaedra so delighted in Hippolytus, Ariadne in Theseus, Thisbe in her Pyramus, as she is enamoured on her Mopsus.

l.hi: Be thou the Marigold, and I will be the Sun,

lg.l: Be thou the Friar, and I will be the Nun.

div.p: I could repeat centuries of such. Now tell me what greater dotage, or blindness can there be than this in both sexes? And yet their slavery is more eminent, a greater sign of their folly than the rest.

They are commonly slaves, captives, voluntary servants, Amator amicae mancipium [the lover, slave of his girlfriend], as Lib. 3 de aulico.Castilio terms him, his Mistress’ servant, her drudge, prisoner, bondman, what not? He composeth himself wholly to her affections, to please her; and as Emilia said, makes himself her lackey. All his cares, actions, all his thoughts, are subordinate to her will and commandment; her most devote, obsequious, affectionate servant and vassal. For love (as Cyroped. lib. 5.Cyrus in Xenophon well observed) is a mere tyranny, worse than any disease, and they that are troubled with it, desire to be free and cannot, but are harder bound than if they were in iron chains. What greater captivity or slavery can there be (as In paradoxis.Tully expostulates) than to be in love? Is he a free man over whom a woman domineers, to whom she prescribes Laws, commands, forbids what she will herself? That dares deny nothing she demands; she asks, he gives; she calls, he comes; she threatens, he fears; nequissimum hunc servum puto, I account this man a very drudge. And as he follows it, Is this no small servitude for an enamorate to be every hour combing his head, stiffening his beard, perfuming his hair, washing his face with sweet waters, painting, curling, and not to come abroad but sprucely crowned, decked and apparelled? Yet these are but toys in respect to go to the Barber, Baths, Theatres, &c., he must attend upon her wherever she goes, run along the streets by her doors and windows to see her, take all opportunities, sleeveless errands, disguise,
counterfeit shapes, and as many forms as Jupiter himself ever took; and come every day to her house (as he will surely do if he be truly enamoured) and offer her service, and follow her up and down from room to room, as Lucretia’s suitors did, he cannot contain himself but he will do it, he must and will be where she is, sit next her, still talking with her. If I did but let my glove fall by chance (as the said Aretine’s Lucretia brags), I had one of my suitors, nay two or three at once ready to stoop and take it up, and kiss it, and with a long congee deliver it unto me: if I would walk, another was ready to sustain me by the arm. A third to provide fruits, Pears, Plums, Cherries, or whatsoever I would eat or drink. All this and much more he doth in her presence, and when he comes home, as Troilus on his Criseyde, ’tis all his meditation to recount with himself her actions, words, gestures, what entertainment he had, how kindly she used him in such a place, how she smiled, how she graced him, and that infinitely pleased him; then he breaks out, O sweet Areusa, O my dearest Antiphila, O most divine looks, O lovely graces, and thereupon instantly he makes an Epigram, or a Sonnet to five or seven tunes, in her commendation, or else he ruminates how she rejected his service, denied him a kiss, disgraced him, &c., and that as effectually torments him. And these are his exercises betwixt comb and glass, Madrigals, Elegies, &c., these his cogitations till he see her again. But all this is easy and gentle, and the least part of his labour and bondage, no hunter will take such pains for his Game, Fowler for his sport, or Soldier to sack a City, as he will for his Mistress’ favour.

l.hi: Ipsa comes veniam, neque me salebrosa movebunt
Saxa, nec obliquo dente timendus aper,

lg.l: [I’ll come myself as your partner; the rugged rocks
Won’t trouble me, nor the fearsome boar’s skewed tusk,]

div.p: as Phaedra to Hippolytus. No danger shall affright; for if that be true the Poets feign, Love is the son of Mars and Venus; as he hath delights, pleasures, elegancies from his mother, so hath he hardness, valour and boldness from his father. And ’tis true that Bernard hath; amore nihil mollius, nihil violentius, nothing so boisterous, nothing so tender as love. If once therefore enamoured, he will go, run, ride many a mile to meet her, day and night, in a very dark night, endure scorching heat, cold, wait in frost and snow, rain, tempests, till his teeth chatter in his head, those Northern winds and showers cannot cool or quench his flames of love. Intempesta nocte non deterretur [He’s not deterred by the dead of night], he will, take my word, he will sustain hunger, thirst, penetrabit omnia, perrumpet omnia [he’ll force his way into everything, will break through everything], love will find out a way, through thick and thin he will to her; expeditissimi montes videntur, amnes tranabiles [mountains seem eminently climbable, rivers seem swimmable], he will swim through an Ocean, ride post over the Alps, Apennine, or Pyrenean hills,

l.hi: Ignem marisque fluctus, atque turbines

lg.l: Venti paratus est transire, ———
[He’s prepared to pass through fire and billowing seas
And whirling winds …]

div.p: though it rain daggers with their points downward, light or dark, all is one:

lg.l: (Roscida per tenebras Faunus ad antra venit)
[Faunus came through the shadows to the dewy caves]

div.p:
for her sweet sake he will undertake Hercules’ twelve labours, endure hazard, &c., he feels it not. Lib. 1 de contem. amor.What shall I say (saith Haedus) of their great dangers they undergo, single combats they undertake, how they will venture their lives, creep in at windows, gutters, climb over walls to come to their sweethearts (anointing the doors and hinges with oil, because they should not creak, tread soft, swim, wade, watch, &c.), and if they be surprised, leap out at windows, cast themselves headlong down, bruising or breaking their legs or arms, and sometimes losing life itself, as Calisto did for his lovely Melibea. Hear some of their own confessions, protestations, complaints, proffers, expostulations, wishes, brutish attempts, labours in this kind. Hercules served Omphale, put on an apron, took a distaff and spun; Thraso the soldier was so submiss to Thais, that he was resolved to do whatsoever she enjoined. Ter. Eunuch. Act. 5 Scen. 8.Ego me Thaidi dedam, & faciam quod jubet [I’ll surrender myself to Thais and do what she commands], I am at her service. Philostratus in an Epistle to his Mistress, I am ready to die Sweetheart if it be thy will; allay his thirst whom thy star hath scorched and undone, the fountains and rivers deny no man drink that comes; the fountain doth not say thou shalt not drink, nor the apple thou shalt not eat, nor the fair meadow walk not in me, but thou alone wilt not let me come near thee, or see thee, contemned and despised I die for grief. Polyaenus when his Mistress Circe did but frown upon him in Petronius, drew his sword, and bade her kill, stab, or whip him to death, he would strip himself naked, and not resist. Another will take a journey to Japan, longae navigationis molestias non curans [not caring about the discomforts of a long journey]; a third (if she say it) will not speak a word for a twelvemonth’s space, her command shall be most inviolably kept: a fourth will take Hercules’ club from him, and with that Centurion in the Spanish Act. 15 & 18.Celestina, will kill ten men for his Mistress Areusa, for a word of her mouth, he will cut bucklers in two like pippins, and flap down men like flies, Elige quo mortis genere illum occidi cupis? [would you choose how you’d like him to be killed?] Gaspar Ens.Galeatus of Mantua did a little more: for when he was almost mad for love of a fair Maid in the City, she to try him belike what he would do for her sake, bade him in jest leap into the River Po if he loved her; he forthwith did leap headlong off the bridge and was drowned. Another at Ticinum in like passion, when his Mistress by chance (thinking no harm I dare swear) bade him go hang, the next night at her doors hanged himself. In sympos.Money (saith Xenophon) is a very acceptable and welcome guest, yet I had rather give it my dear
Cleinias, than take it of others, I had rather serve him, than command others, I had rather be his drudge, than take my ease, undergo any danger for his sake, than live in security.
